description: American settlements take root and stay on the map from their founding year onward, growing into major cities as reflected in periodic census counts.

events.title: New York City founded
events.desc: Dutch colonists established a fur-trading settlement at the tip of Manhattan Island; it would be renamed New York after the English took control in 1664.

events.title: Boston founded
events.desc: Puritan colonists settled the Shawmut Peninsula, founding what became the political and commercial center of New England.

events.title: Charleston founded
events.desc: English colonists established Charles Town, which grew into the wealthiest and most cosmopolitan city in the colonial South.

events.title: Philadelphia founded
events.desc: William Penn laid out the city on land granted by the English crown, planning it on a grid as a haven for religious dissenters.

events.title: New Orleans founded
events.desc: French colonists established the port city near the mouth of the Mississippi, which passed to Spanish and then back to French control before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.

events.title: San Antonio founded
events.desc: Spanish colonists established a mission and presidio along the San Antonio River; the settlement grew into the largest town in Spanish and later Mexican Texas.

events.title: Baltimore founded
events.desc: The town was chartered on the Patapsco River as a tobacco-shipping port for the Maryland colony.

events.title: St. Louis founded
events.desc: French fur traders established a trading post on the Mississippi, which later became a key jumping-off point for westward expeditions and migration.

events.title: San Francisco founded
events.desc: Spain established a fort and mission on the San Francisco Bay, the seed of a small settlement that stayed modest for seven decades.

events.title: Los Angeles founded
events.desc: Spanish colonial authorities established a small farming pueblo, decades before it became part of Mexico and, later, the United States.

events.title: Cincinnati founded
events.desc: Settlers established a town on the Ohio River that grew rapidly as a meatpacking and manufacturing center, earning the nickname "Porkopolis."

events.title: Baltimore: population 16,359
events.desc: Baltimore was already among the five largest cities in the new republic.

events.title: Boston: population 18,320
events.desc: Boston ranked as the fourth-largest city in the young United States.

events.title: Charleston: population 13,503
events.desc: Charleston ranked among the five largest cities in the country, built on rice, indigo, and the trade in enslaved people; its relative rank fell over the next century as inland and western cities outgrew it.

events.title: New York City: population 33,131
events.desc: The first US census recorded New York as the country's largest city, a rank it has held in every census since.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 28,522
events.desc: Philadelphia was the new nation's second-largest city and, for a time, its capital.

events.title: New Orleans: population 17,000
events.desc: Now under US control, New Orleans was already a major port for cotton and sugar shipped down the Mississippi.

events.title: St. Louis: population 1,400
events.desc: St. Louis remained a small frontier river town in the years just after the Louisiana Purchase.

events.title: New York City: population 202,589
events.desc: New York passed the 200,000 mark, its growth fueled by the newly opened Erie Canal, which routed western trade through the port.

events.title: Chicago founded
events.desc: The settlement at the mouth of the Chicago River, with only a few hundred residents, was formally incorporated as a town; it became a city just four years later.

events.title: Houston founded
events.desc: Brothers Augustus and John Allen founded the town on Buffalo Bayou and named it for Sam Houston shortly after his victory at San Jacinto; it briefly served as capital of the Republic of Texas.

events.title: Austin founded
events.desc: The Republic of Texas relocated its capital to a small settlement then known as Waterloo, renaming it for empresario Stephen F. Austin.

events.title: San Francisco: population 900
events.desc: Just before gold was discovered nearby, the renamed town of San Francisco was still a sleepy port of a few hundred people.

events.title: Austin: population 629
events.desc: As the seat of Texas's government, Austin remained a small frontier town on the edge of settled territory.

events.title: Baltimore: population 169,054
events.desc: Rail and shipping trade made Baltimore the country's second-largest city for a time in the mid-1800s.

events.title: Boston: population 136,881
events.desc: Landfill projects steadily expanded the peninsula's buildable area as the population grew.

events.title: Chicago: population 29,963
events.desc: Rail lines converging on Chicago were turning it into the Midwest's dominant transportation hub.

events.title: Cincinnati: population 115,435
events.desc: Cincinnati had become one of the largest cities in the country, rivaling the older cities of the East Coast.

events.title: Houston: population 2,396
events.desc: Houston remained a modest bayou town, still well behind San Antonio and the port of Galveston in size.

events.title: Los Angeles: population 1,610
events.desc: At the time of California statehood, Los Angeles was still a small, dusty ranching town, far smaller than San Francisco to the north.

events.title: New Orleans: population 116,375
events.desc: New Orleans ranked among the five largest US cities, its port among the busiest in the country.

events.title: New York City: population 515,547
events.desc: The city more than doubled in two decades as immigration surged, especially from Ireland and Germany.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 121,376
events.desc: Manufacturing and shipbuilding drove steady growth through the first half of the century.

events.title: San Antonio: population 3,488
events.desc: San Antonio was already Texas's largest town, its economy built on ranching and a population mixing Tejano, German, and Anglo settlers.

events.title: San Francisco: population 34,776
events.desc: The Gold Rush transformed the town almost overnight into a booming, chaotic city of prospectors, merchants, and speculators.

events.title: St. Louis: population 77,860
events.desc: Steamboat trade on the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers fueled explosive growth in just a few decades.

events.title: Austin: population 3,494
events.desc: Austin's population grew more than fivefold in a decade as the state government and surrounding ranching economy expanded.

events.title: San Antonio: population 8,235
events.desc: Heavy German immigration helped San Antonio become the largest town in Texas, ahead of the Gulf port of Galveston.

events.title: Chicago: population 298,977
events.desc: Chicago's population had grown roughly tenfold in twenty years, driven by railroads, stockyards, and manufacturing.

events.title: New York City: population 1,206,299
events.desc: New York became the first US city recorded with over a million residents.

events.title: San Antonio: population 20,550
events.desc: The arrival of the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway in 1877 opened a new era of growth for the city.

events.title: Austin: population 22,258
events.desc: Austin had grown into a modest state capital, still far smaller than Texas's commercial hubs of San Antonio, Houston, and Galveston.

events.title: Baltimore: population 508,957
events.desc: Baltimore had grown into a major manufacturing and port city on the East Coast.

events.title: Boston: population 560,892
events.desc: Boston had grown into a major industrial and financial center, though it slipped in national rank as western cities boomed.

events.title: Chicago: population 1,698,575
events.desc: Rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1871, Chicago had become the country's second-largest city.

events.title: Cincinnati: population 325,902
events.desc: Growth continued but at a slower pace as rail hubs further west, like Chicago, drew trade away.

events.title: Houston: population 44,633
events.desc: Railroads converging on Houston were turning it into a major commercial center, just before the nearby Spindletop oil discovery transformed the regional economy.

events.title: Los Angeles: population 102,479
events.desc: Rail connections and land promotion sparked rapid growth in the late 1800s, setting up the city's explosive twentieth-century expansion.

events.title: New Orleans: population 287,104
events.desc: Growth slowed relative to northern and midwestern rivals, though the port remained economically vital.

events.title: New York City: population 3,437,202
events.desc: The 1898 consolidation with Brooklyn and other boroughs into Greater New York nearly tripled the city's official population overnight.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 1,293,697
events.desc: Philadelphia remained the country's third-largest city, behind only New York and Chicago.

events.title: San Antonio: population 53,321
events.desc: San Antonio was Texas's largest city, its cattle-trail and railroad connections drawing steady growth.

events.title: San Francisco: population 342,782
events.desc: San Francisco had become the largest and most important city on the West Coast.

events.title: St. Louis: population 575,238
events.desc: St. Louis had grown into the fourth-largest city in the country ahead of hosting the 1904 World's Fair.
